name: Cash Flow Forecasting
title: Cash Flow Forecasting
answer: Cash flow forecasting in treasury and liquidity covers predicting future cash positions across operating, investing, and financing activities to ensure the company can meet obligations and deploy surplus. It spans short-term daily or weekly liquidity forecasts and longer horizon planning for debt, investment, and capital allocation. The AI accountant treats this as a core treasury function where forecast accuracy directly affects borrowing costs, covenant headroom, and working capital.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Cash flow forecasting in treasury and liquidity covers predicting future cash positions across operating, investing, and financing activities to ensure the company can meet obligations and deploy surplus. It spans short-term daily or weekly liquidity forecasts and longer horizon planning for debt, investment, and capital allocation. The AI accountant treats this as a core treasury function where forecast accuracy directly affects borrowing costs, covenant headroom, and working capital.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the treasury management system and enterprise resource planning data, including bank balances, payables, receivables, payroll, tax, and intercompany flows. Forecast models typically sit in a cloud data warehouse or a dedicated cash forecasting module that pulls from bank APIs and ERP extracts on a scheduled basis. Compute needs are modest compared with large language model training, so a standard business analytics stack with automated data pipelines is usually sufficient.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by combining statistical time series models, such as exponential smoothing or gradient boosted trees, with rules that encode known payment dates and contractual terms. Machine learning models learn patterns in customer payment timing, supplier disbursement, and seasonal demand, then generate a distribution of expected cash balances rather than a single point estimate. Treasury analysts review exceptions, adjust for one-off events, and compare actuals to forecast to retrain or recalibrate the model.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk and provenance center on data quality, model explainability, and segregation of duties. Forecasts used for liquidity decisions must be traceable to source transactions, and the model should expose which drivers, such as days sales outstanding or payroll timing, moved the prediction. Access to forecast outputs and override rights are typically restricted, with an audit trail showing who changed an assumption and why, because a wrong liquidity forecast can trigger covenant breaches or unnecessary borrowing.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Where it is going is toward continuous, event-driven forecasting that updates as invoices, payments, and market rates change, rather than on a fixed daily or weekly cycle. More treasury teams are testing scenario engines that link cash forecasts to supply chain disruptions, interest rate moves, and customer credit deterioration. The likely near-term shift is from explaining what cash will be to recommending specific actions, such as drawing a credit line, delaying a disbursement batch, or sweeping excess cash, with a human approving the action.
